examDifficulty.heading: Is the Technical Architect Review Board Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is the final stage of CTA and the hardest assessment Salesforce runs. You are given an enterprise scenario, design a complete solution, then present and defend it to a panel of judges who are themselves CTAs. There is no question paper and no partial credit for knowing the platform.
bullets: A live defence, not an exam. You present your architecture and answer sustained questioning.
Judged by practising CTAs. The decision is the panel's, against the areas the scenario requires you to cover.
Entry is gated. You must hold both architect credentials and have passed the evaluation stage.
Fee: third-party sources put this stage at around US$4,500, separate from the evaluation. Confirm current fees with Salesforce.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Candidates who pass have almost always sat several mock boards with practising CTAs. If you have never had a design pulled apart out loud, you are not ready, however strong your platform knowledge is.

examFormat.heading: Technical Architect Review Board Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The board is a presentation and defence built on a scenario. Here is what the day involves:
bestWayToPass: Use a fixed running order: Data, security and sharing, integration, development lifecycle, licensing. Cover it the same way every time so nothing is dropped under pressure.
Lead with the business outcome: Say what the design achieves before how it works. Judges assess whether a business audience could follow you.
Pre-empt the obvious challenges: Name the weak points yourself, with the mitigation, before a judge finds them.
Rehearse hostile questioning: The questioning is where most candidates come apart. Practise being interrupted.

practiceQuestionsIntroSuffix: — practice thinking like a CTA and defending architecture decisions for the Review Board.

certificationCard.description: The final stage of CTA. You receive an enterprise scenario, design a full solution, then present and defend it to a panel of Certified Technical Architects. Passing earns the credential.

keyConcepts.h2: CTA Review Board: Key Concepts for Preparation

blocks.heading: The Format of the Day
blocks.body: You are given a scenario describing a company: its business goals, existing systems, constraints and pain points. You prepare a solution architecture, then present it to a panel of judges. The presentation is followed by extended questioning, where judges probe the parts of the design they find weakest. They are not trying to catch you out on trivia. They are testing whether your design holds together, whether you understood the requirements, and whether you can reason about it under pressure. The outcome is the panel's judgement against the areas the scenario demands, not a percentage.

blocks.heading: Preparing the Architecture
blocks.body: Design for the scenario in front of you, not for a textbook enterprise. Cover the data model and how it handles the volumes described, how records are secured and shared including any external users, how the systems integrate and in which direction, how changes are built and released, and which licences the design implies. Prefer standard capability and justify every departure from it. Keep the solution proportionate: unnecessary components are not neutral, because each one is something a judge can ask about and something you must defend.

blocks.heading: Presenting Clearly
blocks.body: Judges sit through many presentations, and clarity carries weight. Start with the business outcome and the shape of the solution, then go through your running order. Use diagrams that can be read at a glance and that you can talk through without reciting. Keep to time: running out before you reach licensing or release management means those areas go uncovered. Speak as if the audience includes the sponsor who would pay for this, because the ability to explain architecture to a business audience is explicitly part of what is assessed.

blocks.heading: Handling the Questioning
blocks.body: This is where most candidates are decided. Expect judges to challenge your choices, propose alternatives and introduce complications. For each significant decision, know the requirement it serves, the alternative you rejected, and the cost you accepted. When a challenge is sound, acknowledge it and adjust: that reads as judgement. When it is not, defend your position calmly with the reasoning. Both instant capitulation and refusal to engage are negative signals. Saying you do not know, then explaining how you would find out, is better than inventing an answer.

blocks.heading: Common Reasons Candidates Fail
blocks.body: Four patterns recur. **Missed requirements:** a strong design that does not address something the scenario asked for. **Unjustified choices:** components on the diagram the candidate cannot explain. **No acknowledged trade-offs:** presenting the design as having no downsides, which suggests it was not analysed. **Poor time management:** running out before covering every area. Notice that none of these is a knowledge gap. Candidates reach this stage having passed seven exams; what separates passes from failures is judgement and delivery.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Technical Architect Review Board Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The board tests whether you can design under constraints and defend it to people who will push back. Preparation means rehearsal, not revision.

blocks.heading: A Fixed Running Order
blocks.body: Data, security and sharing, integration, lifecycle, licensing. The same order every time means nothing gets forgotten when the clock is against you.

blocks.heading: Justify Every Component
blocks.body: If it is on the diagram, be ready to say which requirement put it there and what you considered instead.

blocks.heading: Name Your Own Weaknesses
blocks.body: Raising a trade-off before a judge does shows analysis. Claiming there are none shows the opposite.

blocks.heading: Answer the Question Asked
blocks.body: Under pressure it is tempting to retreat to what you rehearsed. Judges notice when an answer does not address the challenge.

blocks.heading: Mock Boards
blocks.body: Practise with people who will interrupt and disagree. It is the single highest-value preparation for this stage.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the review board session consist of?
options: Presenting a solution to a given scenario and defending it under questioning
A written document submitted in advance
A 60-question multiple-choice exam
A hands-on configuration task completed in a live Salesforce org
sampleQuestions.explanation: Candidates present their architecture to a panel and then face extended questioning on it.
whyWrong: A document alone is not the assessment; the defence is central.
There is no multiple-choice component at the board.
There is no hands-on build.

sampleQuestions.question: A judge proposes an alternative to the candidate's integration approach, and the argument is sound. What is the best response?
options: Acknowledge the point and adjust
Defend the original choice regardless
Apologise and ask the judge to decide
Change the requirement so the original design fits
sampleQuestions.explanation: Reasoned adjustment in the face of a good argument demonstrates the judgement being assessed.
whyWrong: Refusing to move on a sound objection reads as inflexibility.
Deferring the decision abandons the architect's role.
Requirements are fixed; the design must serve them.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate finishes the presentation without covering licensing or release management. Why does this matter?
options: It does not matter if the data model is strong
Those areas go unassessed
The judges will cover them afterwards
It only affects the fee
sampleQuestions.explanation: The panel judges whether the required areas were addressed. Running out of time leaves gaps that count against you.
whyWrong: One strong area does not compensate for missing others.
The candidate is responsible for covering the ground.
Fees are unrelated to performance.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes what the panel is assessing?
options: How quickly the candidate speaks
Judgement: coverage, justification, trade-offs, risk and communication
The visual design of the slides
Recall of Salesforce feature names and the platform limits that apply
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform knowledge is assumed from the prerequisites. The board assesses the reasoning built on top of it.
whyWrong: Pace matters only insofar as it affects clarity and coverage.
Readable diagrams help, but polish is not the criterion.
Feature recall was tested by the seven prerequisite exams.

sampleQuestions.question: What must be true before a candidate can sit the review board?
options: They have worked at Salesforce
They have completed at least one relevant Trailhead superbadge
They hold both architect credentials and have passed the evaluation stage
They hold the Administrator credential
sampleQuestions.explanation: Both architect credentials are prerequisites, and the evaluation stage gates access to the board.
whyWrong: There is no employer requirement.
Superbadges are not part of the CTA path.
Administrator is far below the requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate is asked about a component they included but cannot explain. What does this cost them?
options: Nothing at all, because extra components demonstrate useful breadth
It improves the score for ambition
Credibility, because every element of the design should be justifiable
Only time, not marks
sampleQuestions.explanation: Unjustified components invite questions the candidate cannot answer, which undermines the whole defence.
whyWrong: Breadth without justification is a liability, not a strength.
Ambition is not a criterion.
It affects the judgement, not just the clock.

sampleQuestions.question: How should a candidate open the presentation?
options: With a list naming every single Salesforce product used in the design
With the business outcome and the overall shape of the solution
With an apology for the time constraints
With the governor limits that apply
sampleQuestions.explanation: Leading with the outcome lets the panel follow the reasoning, and the ability to explain to a business audience is assessed.
whyWrong: A product list does not explain what the solution achieves.
Apologising wastes the time available.
Limits are detail, not the opening frame.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate does not know the answer to a detailed question about a product's behaviour. What is the best response?
options: Invent a plausible-sounding answer
Blame the scenario for being unclear
Say so, then explain how they would establish the answer
Change the subject across to an area of the design that is stronger
sampleQuestions.explanation: Admitting a gap and describing how you would resolve it is treated far better than a confident invention.
whyWrong: Judges are practising CTAs and will recognise an invented answer.
Blaming the scenario does not answer it.
Avoiding the question is obvious to the panel.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is a common reason candidates fail the board?
options: Producing a strong design that misses a stated requirement
Finishing the presentation early
Using standard Salesforce features
Knowing a great deal too much about enterprise integration patterns
sampleQuestions.explanation: Missed requirements are among the most frequent failures, because coverage is fundamental to the judgement.
whyWrong: Finishing early is fine if everything was covered.
Standard features are preferred over custom build.
Depth is an advantage, not a problem.

sampleQuestions.question: Why is a fixed running order recommended?
options: It shortens the session
It replaces the need for diagrams
It guarantees that the judges will not ask any further questions at all
It makes coverage of every required area automatic under time pressure
sampleQuestions.explanation: A rehearsed order means data, security, integration, lifecycle and licensing are all addressed without relying on memory.
whyWrong: The session length is set by the format.
Diagrams remain central.
Questioning follows regardless of structure.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the right attitude to trade-offs in the presentation?
options: Avoid mentioning any weakness
List all of the trade-offs but offer no mitigation for any of them
Name them yourself, with the mitigation, before a judge raises them
Claim the design has no downsides
sampleQuestions.explanation: Raising trade-offs with mitigations demonstrates that the design was analysed rather than assembled.
whyWrong: Hidden weaknesses are found during questioning anyway.
Naming problems without mitigations is only half the work.
A design with no stated downsides suggests no analysis.

sampleQuestions.question: Who sits on the panel?
options: Automated assessment software
Practising Certified Technical Architects
Salesforce sales representatives
Other candidates who are also taking the board that day
sampleQuestions.explanation: The board is judged by people who hold the credential and have done the work.
whyWrong: It is a live human assessment.
The assessment is technical, not commercial.
Candidates are assessed individually, not by peers.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate's design uses custom code where a standard feature would serve. How should they handle it at the board?
options: Remove the requirement it addresses
Argue that custom code is always a more flexible choice than standard features
Present it without comment
Be ready to justify why the standard feature was unsuitable, or change the design
sampleQuestions.explanation: Custom build needs a reason. Without one, the standard capability is the expected answer.
whyWrong: Requirements cannot be removed.
Flexibility does not justify the maintenance cost on its own.
Unexplained custom build is exactly what questioning will target.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the most valuable preparation for the questioning section?
options: Mock boards with people who interrupt and challenge the design
Reading a good deal more of the official Salesforce documentation
Preparing longer slides
Memorising the scenario format
sampleQuestions.explanation: The questioning tests defending a design live, a skill built only by being challenged in practice.
whyWrong: Documentation covers knowledge, which is already assumed.
Longer slides reduce the time available to defend.
The format is not what decides the result.

sampleQuestions.question: How is the outcome decided?
options: By an automated rubric with no human input
By the length of the candidate's experience
By a percentage score calculated across the multiple-choice answers given
By the panel's judgement against the areas the scenario requires
sampleQuestions.explanation: The panel judges the defence against the required areas; there is no percentage mark.
whyWrong: Judges make the decision, not software.
Experience helps you prepare but does not decide the result.
There are no multiple-choice answers to score.
